prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved from B006 to B015, and I want to say why on scientific grounds and not because five colleagues sit there. My own round-1 test was quantitative, reproducible theory tied to measurement. On that test the lattice clock does better than I first allowed. The magic-wavelength condition is a clean, checkable idea: it cancels the trap light shift to the level the clock needs, and the resulting accuracy and stability have been confirmed by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) with agreeing intercomparisons near 1e-18 over about two decades, with no disputed interpretation. The answer to the chair's first question, as I now see it, is that the step beyond 2005 and 2012 is specific: neutral atoms held in a lattice, thousands interrogated at once, which created the many-atom regime, millimetre-scale resolution of gravitational redshift, and many-body effects (spin exchange, SU(N) physics) inside the clock itself. Those are results about quantum matter that follow from the lattice and could not have come from single trapped ions or the comb alone, and my own field of electronic-structure and spin-dynamics theory is already being applied to such many-body clock systems. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the record level. Everyone proposes the same pair.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains novelty and weight of the claim. Frequency metrology was honoured in 2005 and 2012, the redefinition of the second has not happened, and the fundamental-physics payoffs so far are null results that tighten bounds. This is closer to an invention with record performance than to a clue from nature, and Danielsson's discovery-first principle is a legitimate criterion that B015 meets less well than B007 or B006. There is also a credit residue: other Sr and Yb groups and the ion-clock lines contributed, so the citation must be worded around the lattice concept and its realization and not imply a single origin of the clock family. Finally, by moving I give up what I still regard as the best theory-then-experiment chain on the list (B006), and I think the committee should return to it, because the reasons I held it back (unsettled pairing mechanism, Cao outside the names, disorder-limited reproducibility) are about timing, and timing improves.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock differs from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes because it works with neutral atoms in a lattice and created the regime of many-atom clocks, with spin-exchange and SU(N) physics inside the clock, and that the interpretation has never been disputed.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me. I asked in round 1 whether B015 adds enough beyond the two earlier prizes, and your answer is a concrete physical regime that the earlier work did not reach, not a claim of general importance. I would ask that the citation say so, naming the magic-wavelength lattice, so that it reads as the lattice principle and not as a third prize for better clocks. I also accept your caution that the competing ion-clock line is a reason to credit the concept and not a general title such as 'atomic clocks'.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the concept (Katori) and the performance frontier (Ye) map onto two people, that reproduction at 1e-18 across laboratories is the evidence of maturity, and that the citation should not imply a single origin for the clock family. He also notes that the strongest fundamental-physics results so far are null bounds.
responses.response: I agree on the wording and I would add that the null results do not weaken the case, since a precision instrument is judged by systematics checked by others, which is what the intercomparisons provide. I do not think the pending redefinition of the second should be a condition either way: it is supporting evidence that the clocks are mature, and the citation should rest on the invention and the record accuracy. Where I still differ from you is the two-part idea. Pairing B015 with B007 or B057 would import the credit problems of those entries (the IceCube three-name set, Chu and Borde for atom interferometry), and I prefer a single clean prize over a two-part configuration whose second half is not settled.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the secure flat-band prediction plus the discovery of correlated states is sufficient for B006, that delay does not make attribution easier, and that the prize would honour the mechanism and not a theory of pairing.
responses.response: I took your point seriously and I still agree that the flat band and the existence of the correlated phases are not in doubt, and that a carefully worded citation avoids the pairing question. Our disagreement is now only about order. You are right that waiting does not resolve whether Bistritzer, rather than the broader flat-band theory community, anchors the theory, and I do not claim that it will. But Cao, the independent experimental groups and sample-to-sample variation are open in a way the clock evidence is not, and on that basis I place B015 first and B006 as my first alternative. I would support B006 with Cao addressed in a later cycle, and I would not call your case weak.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B007 on a discovery-first principle but calls B015 the safer choice, and says he would test the claim that the lattice clock is a distinct contribution and not assume it.
responses.response: Your demand that the claim be tested, not assumed, was one I shared, and I think Lindroth's many-atom regime together with millimetre redshift resolution passes it. I accept your principle that a prize should favour what nature told us, and that is why I keep B006, which is a discovery of correlated phases, ahead of B055 in my alternatives. I do not think B007 is poorly founded, but the committee has not settled whether Halzen, Karle and Spiering or a pair is correct, and a prize that must begin with an attribution argument is harder to defend this year than a pair on which all eight agree.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the many-atom lattice regime as a step beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or still reads B015 as an increment on settled ground.
Exact priority of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal relative to closely related lattice-clock proposals, and how to weight Ye's many-body clock work, are from memory and unverified.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes recognition timely or early; I treat it as supporting evidence only.
Whether B006 should wait only a few years or whether the open pairing mechanism will keep it from recognition for much longer.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B015: I have no stated personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye and no co-authorship or supervisory link. I note that my group applies theory to MAX IV and ESS spectroscopy and has an interest in many-body ultrafast dynamics, which is a field-level interest and not a tie to the credited names. B006 and B055 are in my broad field of condensed-matter theory, also without personal ties.
